lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Maximum Value
task: Brute force algorithms systematically evaluate every element within a dataset without employing heuristic shortcuts. To identify the maximum value in an array, the algorithm must iteratively inspect each element, maintaining a reference to the largest value encountered.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Initialize a variable, assuming the element at the zeroth index is the maximum value.
2. Implement an iterative construct to traverse the remaining elements in the array.
3. Apply a comparative conditional evaluation. If the current element strictly exceeds the saved maximum, update the reference variable.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `find_max(arr)`.
2. Evaluate if the array is empty. If true, return the string `'Error'`.
3. Initialize a variable `max_val` assigned to `arr[0]`.
4. Iterate through the elements of `arr`.
5. Inside the iteration, implement an `if` block: if the current `item` is `>` than `max_val`, reassign `max_val` to the current `item`.
6. Return `max_val` upon loop termination.
7. Review the Complexity tab. The structural pass identifies a single loop, evaluating the global time complexity as O(n).

lesson_1.title: Brute Force: Minimum Value
task: Isolating the minimum value mirrors the maximum value extraction process with inverted comparative logic. The algorithm evaluates each element sequentially, updating a reference to the smallest observed value.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Initialize a tracking variable with the value of the first array element.
2. Traverse the remaining array elements sequentially.
3. If the evaluated element is strictly less than the tracking variable, execute a reassignment.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `find_min(arr)`.
2. If the array is empty, return the string `'Error'`.
3. Assign `min_val` to the initial element.
4. Iterate through the array. If the current item evaluates as `<` than `min_val`, update the variable.
5. Return `min_val`.

lesson_1.title: Exhaustive Pair Search
task: Identifying combinatorial pairs requires an exhaustive evaluation of all possible element combinations. Implementing a nested iterative structure allows the algorithm to systematically test every discrete pair against a target sum.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Establish an outer iteration to isolate a primary numeric operand.
2. Establish a nested inner iteration to sequentially evaluate all subsequent elements as the secondary operand.
3. If the combined sum equals the specified target, immediately return the Boolean `True`.
4. If the nested iterations terminate without a valid match, return the Boolean `False`.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `has_pair_sum(arr, target)`.
2. Implement an outer loop utilizing index `i` bounding from `0` to the length of `arr`.
3. Nest an inner loop utilizing index `j` bounding from `i + 1` to the length of `arr`.
4. Implement a conditional evaluation: if `arr[i] + arr[j] == target`, execute `return True`.
5. Return `False` outside the iterative constructs.
6. Observe the static complexity evaluation. The nested hierarchy generates an O(n²) Time Complexity.
Sample Output:
has_pair_sum([2, 4, 7, 11], 13) → True

lesson_1.title: Conditional Counting
task: Sequential traversal enables the accumulation of elements satisfying specific conditional criteria. This algorithmic pattern evaluates elements individually, incrementing a persistent state variable upon a positive condition match.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Initialize an accumulation variable at absolute zero.
2. Execute a linear traversal across the array elements.
3. Evaluate each element against a modulo operation to determine parity. If the evaluation asserts as true, increment the accumulator.
4. Return the terminal accumulator state.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `count_evens(arr)`.
2. Initialize a variable `count` to 0.
3. Iterate through `arr`.
4. Implement a modulo operation to evaluate `item % 2 == 0`.
5. If the condition is met, increment `count` by 1.
6. Return the `count` variable.

lesson_1.title: Algorithmic Short-Circuiting
task: Algorithmic short-circuiting terminates loop execution immediately upon satisfying a target objective. While this optimizes empirical runtime by averting unnecessary iterations, the asymptotic worst-case complexity remains bounded linearly.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Initiate a linear traversal of the array elements.
2. Implement a conditional evaluation targeting a specific integer attribute.
3. Upon locating an element satisfying the criteria, trigger an immediate operational return.
4. If the traversal concludes without a positive evaluation, return a defined baseline integer.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `first_negative(arr)`.
2. Iterate linearly through `arr`.
3. If the active `item` evaluates as `< 0`, execute `return item` immediately.
4. Return `0` strictly outside the loop boundary.
5. Note that the static analyzer computes the maximum potential traversal depth, maintaining the Time Complexity at O(n).
Sample Output:
first_negative([5, 3, -2, 8, -1]) → -2

lesson_2.title: Standard Linear Search
task: Linear Search represents the foundational methodology for locating a target variable within an unsorted collection. The algorithm systematically evaluates sequential indices until an equivalency match triggers a return statement.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Initialize index zero as the evaluative starting point.
2. Sequentially compare the active element against the target variable.
3. Upon a positive evaluation, terminate the iteration and return the active index.
4. If the array exhausts without a match, return `-1` to denote failure.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `linear_search(arr, target)`.
2. Construct an iteration sequence utilizing an index `i` bounded by the array length.
3. Implement the condition: if `arr[i] == target`, execute `return i`.
4. Ensure `return -1` executes only if the loop fully completes.

lesson_2.title: Complete Traversal Search
task: Aggregating all occurrences of a target entity prohibits short-circuit execution. The algorithm must compel a comprehensive structural traversal, incrementing an isolated tracking variable for each positive conditional match.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Declare an integer tracking variable initialized to zero.
2. Execute an exhaustive iteration across the array boundaries.
3. Upon validating an elemental match with the target, increment the tracking variable.
4. Return the terminal state of the tracking variable.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `count_occurrences(arr, target)`.
2. Initialize `count = 0`.
3. Iterate through all elements within `arr`.
4. If `item == target` evaluates to true, increment `count` by 1.
5. Return the `count` variable.
Sample Output:
count_occurrences([1, 2, 2, 3], 2) → 2

lesson_2.title: Overwriting Match State
task: To isolate the terminal occurrence of a target entity, the algorithm must suppress premature return execution. Instead, a persistent state variable undergoes continuous reassignment with the active index upon every valid elemental match.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Initialize a state variable to `-1` to denote an unresolved status.
2. Execute an index-based linear traversal across the array.
3. Whenever the element at the active index equals the target variable, assign the active index to the state variable.
4. Return the state variable upon conclusion of the traversal.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `last_occurrence(arr, target)`.
2. Initialize `last_index = -1`.
3. Iterate index `i` from `0` to the sequential limit of `arr`.
4. Under the condition `arr[i] == target`, execute the reassignment `last_index = i`.
5. Return `last_index`.
Sample Output:
last_occurrence([1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4], 2) → 4

lesson_2.title: Bounded Linear Search
task: Search operations can be algorithmically constrained to localized memory segments by defining explicit iteration boundaries. This methodology restricts the evaluative loop to a specified index window.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Instantiate an iterative loop utilizing explicit `start` and `end` integer parameters as execution limits.
2. Evaluate elements sequentially strictly within the declared indices.
3. If an element matches the specified target, execute an immediate index return.
4. Return `-1` if the isolated bounded segment exhausts without yielding a match.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `search_in_range(arr, target, start, end)`.
2. Structure an indexed loop utilizing the `start` and `end` arguments to dictate the traversal bounds.
3. If the evaluation `arr[i] == target` asserts as true, return `i`.
4. Execute `return -1` strictly outside the bounded loop.

lesson_2.title: Multi-Target Space Allocation
task: Retaining the positional indices of multiple target occurrences requires dynamic memory utilization. The algorithm must populate an auxiliary array structure, actively transitioning the spatial complexity from an O(1) constant to an O(n) linear bound.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Instantiate an empty auxiliary array to function as the output structure.
2. Execute a complete array traversal, evaluating each index for equivalency to the specified target.
3. Append matching index values directly into the auxiliary array.
4. Return the populated array upon termination of the loop construct.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `multi_search(arr, target)`.
2. Initialize an empty sequence `results = []`.
3. Traverse index `i` from `0` to the length limit of `arr`.
4. If the condition `arr[i] == target` asserts as true, append the scalar `i` to `results`.
5. Return `results`.
6. Observe the analytical feedback to verify the structural transition to an O(n) Space Complexity.

lesson_3.title: Bubble Sort (Ascending)
task: Bubble Sort operates by iterating sequentially through an array to compare and transpose adjacent elements if they violate the target ascending order. This structural process enforces the continuous rightward propagation of maximum values via O(n²) nested iteration.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Establish an outer iteration loop to govern the total passes required for complete array organization.
2. Establish an inner iteration loop to evaluate adjacent element pairs (`j` and `j+1`).
3. Evaluate the numeric values; if the preceding element exceeds the succeeding element, execute a positional swap.
4. Repeat until the array meets strictly ascending criteria.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `bubble_sort_asc(arr)`.
2. Initialize an outer sequence bounded by index `i` iterating through the total array length.
3. Initialize a nested inner sequence bounded by index `j` iterating up to `length - 1`.
4. Formulate the swap condition: if `arr[j] > arr[j+1]`, mutually reassign their indices.
5. Return the sorted `arr` structure.
6. Verify the diagnostic feedback mapping the nested array traversals to an O(n²) Time Complexity parameter.
Sample Output:

lesson_3.title: Selection Sort (Ascending)
task: Selection Sort fundamentally bifurcates an array into an actively sorted boundary and an unsorted partition. It iteratively traverses the unsorted segment to isolate the absolute minimal value, culminating in a singular frontal index swap per pass.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Initialize an outer iteration tracking index `i`, assuming its elemental value acts as the current minimum.
2. Utilize an inner iteration to scan all subsequent elements occurring after index `i`.
3. If the scan identifies a strictly smaller element, update the tracking index to the new minimal target.
4. Upon internal loop conclusion, transpose the element located at the updated minimal index with the element at index `i`.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `selection_sort_asc(arr)`.
2. Structure an outer loop `i` bounded by the array length. Inside, initialize a variable `min_idx = i`.
3. Structure an inner loop `j` bounded from `i + 1` to the array length. Evaluate if `arr[j] < arr[min_idx]`, subsequently updating `min_idx = j` if true.
4. In the outer loop scope, execute a positional swap between `arr[i]` and `arr[min_idx]`.
5. Return the mutated `arr`.
Sample Output:
selection_sort_asc([5, 2, 8, 1]) → [1, 2, 5, 8]

lesson_3.title: Bubble Sort (Descending)
task: Reconfiguring Bubble Sort for a descending algorithmic array involves an absolute inversion of its comparative evaluation block. Swapping conditions are modified to enforce the systematic rightward propagation of minimum mathematical values.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Retain the structural foundation of the O(n²) nested loop architecture.
2. Evaluate adjacent array pairs. If the preceding index value is mathematically lesser than the succeeding index value, execute a mutual state swap.
3. This procedure actively displaces minimal integers toward the array's terminal boundary.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `bubble_sort_desc(arr)`.
2. Replicate the dual O(n²) loop constructs.
3. Define the inverted condition: execute element transposition if `arr[j] < arr[j+1]`.
4. Process the swaps and return the mutated array.
Sample Output:
bubble_sort_desc([1, 2, 3]) → [3, 2, 1]

lesson_3.title: Selection Sort (Descending)
task: Adapting the Selection Sort methodology to establish a descending order requires modifying the analytical internal scan. The algorithm must now traverse the unsorted partition to actively isolate the absolute maximum value, executing an anterior transposition.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Initialize the primary loop bounded by index `i`, assigning its active index to function as a maximal tracking marker.
2. Traverse the subsequent elements. If a scan isolates an integer strictly greater than the current tracking parameter, update the tracker index.
3. Conclude the iteration by executing an index swap, relocating the maximum element into the active `i` position.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `selection_sort_desc(arr)`.
2. Structure the nested traversal loops. Initialize `max_idx = i`.
3. In the inner scope, define the condition `arr[j] > arr[max_idx]`. Execute the reassignment `max_idx = j` if true.
4. Finalize the operation by transposing `arr[i]` and `arr[max_idx]`.
5. Return the array.
Sample Output:
selection_sort_desc([1, 2, 3]) → [3, 2, 1]

lesson_3.title: Single Pass Evaluation
task: Analyzing the internal mechanics of Bubble Sort clarifies that isolating its inner iteration loop performs a singular algorithmic traversal. This single pass inherently guarantees the absolute maximum element is transposed to the terminal index position in linear time.
Algorithm Steps:
1. Discard the outer iteration architecture indicative of a standard O(n²) Bubble Sort.
2. Maintain the internal iteration loop to enforce a singular linear scan across the element set.
3. Evaluate adjacent integers and process localized mutual index swaps based on comparative state.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `single_pass(arr)`.
2. Implement an iterative loop utilizing index `j` bounded strictly to the `length of arr - 1`.
3. If `arr[j] > arr[j+1]`, compute their transposition.
4. Return the partially organized `arr`. Review the diagnostic analyzer to confirm the execution simplifies to an O(n) Linear Time metric.

optimizations.title: Optimization: Two Sum Iteration
task: The current combinatorial algorithm executes successfully but deploys a suboptimal O(n²) nested loop architecture. The objective is to refactor this sequence into a highly efficient O(n) linear operation.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Review the diagnostic metrics indicating an O(n²) time complexity driven by redundant secondary iteration loops.
2. Completely eliminate the inner traversal loop block (`j`) and its corresponding conditional statements.
3. Instantiate a discrete dictionary map to actively track evaluated integers.
4. Within the single primary iteration, algorithmically compute the required numeric differential corresponding to the active element.
5. If the computed differential exists in the tracking map, output the positive pair state immediately.
6. If absent, append the active integer to the map to permit evaluation in subsequent loop cycles.

optimizations.title: Optimization: Memory in Linear Search
task: The implemented linear search functionally isolates the target variable but structurally allocates unnecessary auxiliary array memory, shifting the algorithmic spatial requirement to an inefficient O(n) threshold.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Analyze the Space Complexity metric. The system flags an O(n) bound generated by continuous appending operations to an auxiliary list structure.
2. Discard all sequential blocks concerning the initialization and population of localized tracking lists.
3. Substitute list appending logic with a direct elemental return block to immediately output matched elements.
4. Review the analytical feedback to verify the architectural Space Complexity has regressed to an optimal O(1) state.

optimizations.title: Optimization: In-Place Bubble Sort
task: The generic implementation of Bubble Sort successfully reorganizes internal integer structures but generates suboptimal array duplications via `arr.copy()`, scaling memory usage to an inefficient O(n).
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Consult the diagnostic feedback outlining an O(n) Spatial configuration resulting from active list cloning protocols.
2. Execute the complete removal of blocks assigned to construct isolated sequential clones (e.g., `temp_arr`).
3. Formulate the swap parameters to exclusively execute positional permutations inside the boundaries of the original parameter array.
4. Verify via the real-time analyzer that omitting structural array cloning reduces the Space Complexity to O(1) Constant.
